# Self-efficacy and Digital Technologies

Originally formulated by @bandura_selfefficacy_1982, self-efficacy is defined as "judgments of how well one can execute courses of action required to deal with prospective situations." (p. 122). This construct is fundamental to human agency, as it help to understand how individuals approach challenges, persist despite setbacks, and develop competence in complex domains. It does so by facilitating the establishment of standards and the attainment of performance accomplishments across learning activities [@bandura_selfefficacy_1995; @steele_stereotype_1995;@bandura_selfefficacy_1997]. 

Self-efficacy has proven to be particularly relevant when it comes to digital technologies learning achievements. A whole thematic research agenda has opened up around self-efficacy role on the adoption of new technologies and the develop of competences on digital environments, although there are scattered efforts when it comes to measuring this construct. Early proposals aims on measuring self-efficacy in general computer domains and specific software application tasks [@compeau_computer_1995;@durndell_computer_2002; @weigel_technical_2014], while other studies focuses more on the online browsing and communication [@eastin_internet_2000a; @hsu_internet_2004]. 

In view of the growing hybridization between computational components and the use of the network for social interaction, the discussion on self-efficacy have centered on the ICT framework, which consider a group of generalized tasks as digital information processing, communication and content creation [@aesaert_exploring_2014; @hatlevik_students_2018] but also more computational skills, such as programming or web development [@rohatgi_role_2016]. 

During the second decade of the 21st century, amidst the internet massification, a broad consensus emerged around the idea that ICT self-efficacy was better understood when distinguishing the different areas of use of technologies [@liang_internet_2008; @papastergiou_enhancing_2010; @aesaert_exploring_2014]. Studies adopting this framework consistently identified contrasting associations with key variables related to competence development: while self-efficacy in areas such as data management, communication, and content creation tended to align positively with broader digital proficiency, self-efficacy in more advanced domains—such as web development and programming—often showed different or even inverse patterns of relationship [@rohatgi_role_2016; @gebhardt_gender_2019; @punter_gender_2017].

@ulfert-blank_assessing_2022 pushed the boundaries of the traditional ICT self-efficacy framework by highlighting its limited capacity to keep pace with the rapidly evolving nature of digital systems. Due to the accelerated rate of technological change, many ICT self-efficacy items quickly became obsolete as the applications, functions, or devices they referenced fell out of use. In response to this problem, @ulfert-blank_assessing_2022 proposed the development of updated constructs under the label of digital self-efficacy (DSE), grounded in the most recent guidelines for Digital Competence development, particularly those outlined in the DigComp 2.1 framework [@europeancommissionjointresearchcentre_digcomp_2022]. DigComp emphasizes that constructs related to digital engagement must encompass a wide range of functions and tasks across entire digital systems in order to remain coherent over time and across diverse technological ecologies.

The problem is that the bidimensional aproach to self-efficacy is no longer suitable with recent definitions of Digital competence. New critical competences beyond the informational, communicative, and creative dimensions have begun to be incorporated, specifically safety (i.e., the ability to protect personal data, privacy, and digital well-being while navigating online environments) and problem-solving (i.e., the capacity to diagnose and resolve technical issues, adapt to unfamiliar digital tools, and strategically select appropriate technological solutions). With the introduction of these new types of activity, the DigComp framework tends to favor a multidimensional perspective that organises digital tasks by competence areas rather than by general or specialized use associated with each task [@ulfert-blank_assessing_2022].

Considering the disagreement that exists regarding the dimensionality of digital self-efficacy, it is necessary to study how this conceptual discussion has been adressed by large-scale measurements, as well as the different understandings of self-efficacy that each of them has.

# ICILS and the bi-dimensional DSE

The International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS), conducted by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA), stands as the primary large-scale assessment to explicitly adopt and maintain a bidimensional approach to ICT self-efficacy. ICILS aims to measure students' Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) through standardized performance tests while simultaneously examining the influence of social background variables on digital proficiency. The study has been conducted in three waves —2013, 2018, and 2023— involving large representative samples of 8th-grade students across various educational systems.

Conceptually, ICILS grounds its measurement in social cognitive theory, viewing ICT self-efficacy as a dynamic judgment of one’s capability to organize and execute courses of action [@fraillon_iea_2025a; @bandura_perceived_1993]. Within this framework, the assessment explicitly adopts a task-oriented perspective, differentiating between two distinct dimensions of digital confidence since its inception. The study distinguishes between self-efficacy in general ICT tasks —which reflects confidence in performing everyday activities such as information retrieval and content creation— and self-efficacy in specialized ICT tasks, which targets more complex computational operations like programming or database management [@fraillon_iea_2025a]. By operationalizing these constructs separately, ICILS acknowledges that confidence in routine digital interactions functions as a psychological factor distinct from the self-efficacy required for high-level technical creation.

While the bidimensional structure has remained stable, the specific composition of the batteries has evolved across cycles to mirror the changing digital landscape. Between 2013 and 2018, the terminology shifted from “basic” and “advanced” to “general” and “specialized”, accompanied by a recalibration of items: the general dimension expanded to include tasks like software installation, while the specialized dimension shrank, discarding obsolescent tasks such as virus removal. The 2023 cycle introduced more profound modifications. While the specialized dimension was further narrowed to focus almost exclusively on programming and web creation (e.g., visual and text-based coding), moving away from earlier items related to local networks or database management, the general dimension was updated to incorporate critical information literacy tasks, such as finding original sources. Furthermore, item stems were rephrased to remove explicit references to "computers," acknowledging the diversity of modern devices. Crucially, the measurement scale was also refined, transitioning from a three-point capability scale to a four-point mastery scale (ranging from “I do not think I could do this” to “Very well”), allowing for more granular distinctions in students' self-assessments.

Beyond theoretical justifications, the bidimensional structure of ICT self-efficacy has been supported by robust psychometric validation across all three ICILS cycles, although the specific analytical strategies have evolved to reflect advancements in large-scale assessment methodology. In the inaugural 2013 cycle, the internal structure of the batteries was validated using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) within a Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) framework, which confirmed that the distinction between basic and advanced tasks represented two separate latent factors [@fraillon_icils_2015]. The 2018 cycle further strengthened this evidence by incorporating Multi-group CFA (MGCFA), allowing for a rigorous assessment of measurement invariance to ensure that the general and specialized constructs were comparable across diverse educational systems [@fraillon_iea_2020]. In the most recent 2023 cycle, the assessment shifted away from the SEM framework, adopting Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to verify dimensionality and transitioning to a pure Item Response Theory (IRT) approach. Specifically, the study employed Partial Credit Models (PCM) and Multi-group PCM to establish scale validity and cross-national comparability through fit indices such as RMSD and WRMSD [@fraillon_iea_2025]. Collectively, these rigorous analyses consistently justify the decision to operationalize digital self-efficacy as two distinct, albeit related, constructs.

# Competences area grouped on a unidimensional DSE on PISA

PISA mide autoeficacia como un proxy a competencias digitales, considerando las tareas por area de competencia.

Esto se debe ya que PISA está basado en el DIGCOMP del European Framework. Eso añade novedades a las mediciones de autoeficacia digital.

Sin embargo, PISA tiene muchas similitudes con ICILS, ya que los ítems tienen dimensiones muy parecidas y fraseos similares. Pero se agregan cosas nuevas como problem solving, safety, y tareas contextuales en el aula.

From Self-efficacy agenda document:

"PISA has an ICT assessment framework, which considers 3 dimensions: ICT uses; ICT access and ICT competencies of students. The latter specifies the most relevant competencies identified in existing assessment frameworks on digital literacy. It is worth mentioning that the framework provided by PISA goes in the direction of laying the foundations for, in the future, being able to integrate ICT literacy as a specific domain in its study. Therefore, the document defines ICT literacy as “the interest, attitude and ability of individuals to appropriately use digital technologies and communication tools to access, manage, integrate and evaluate information, construct new knowledge, and communicate with others in order to participate effectively in society” (Lenon et al., 2003, as cited in OECD, 2023). This definition is not original to PISA, but resorts to the conceptualization of Lenon et al. (2003).

ICT competencies include knowledge, understanding, attitudes, dispositions and skills. Self-efficacy is among the attitudes and dispositions towards ICT. In greater depth, the 5 main areas of ICT competencies are: accessing, managing and evaluating information and data (1); sharing information and communicating (2); transforming and creating digital content (3); individual and collaborative problem solving in digital contexts, and computational thinking (4); appropriate use of ICT (knowledge and skills related to safety, security and risk awareness) (5). In this context, it is made explicit that the measure of self-efficacy is the main assessment instrument for ICT competencies.

It is worth mentioning that PISA does not explicitly define “digital self-efficacy” but treats self-efficacy throughout the document in the framework of attitudes and dispositions towards ICT, so that a specific concept of self-efficacy is absent (see p. 277, OECD, 2023)."

# Country level and Gender

When comparing psychological or educational constructs across social groups or countries, the issue of measurement invariance becomes an indispensable methodological requirement. As recent scholarship shows, social science research often assumes—incorrectly—that instruments capture the same underlying meaning across culturally or structurally diverse populations, even though socialization trajectories, interpretive repertoires, and institutional conditions can substantially alter how individuals understand and respond to items [@davidov_measurement_2014;@leitgob_measurement_2023]. 

The contrast between the dimensionality of DSE on both studies is not a matter of chance when it comes to evaluating the sociocultural context in which they are embedded. Available evidence suggests that the magnitude and direction of DSE vary significantly between countries, indicating that self-efficacy is not expressed uniformly but is mediated by social expectations [@gebauer_crosscultural_2021], and differential degrees of exposure to technologies [@hatlevik_students_2018; @senkbeil_ictrelated_2022]. Education systems may associate divergent meanings with seemingly similar tasks with technologies, whether due to contrasting curricular trajectories [@martin-parraga_selfperception_2023; @annemann_teachers_2025], heterogeneity in access to digital infrastructure or differences in the social valuation of certain technological skills [@annemann_teachers_2025; @conte_unlocking_2025].

Differences between-countries on DSE cannot be assumed without first examining the metric equivalence of the construct by study. ICILS has published reports that validate the two-dimensionality of its construct across countries in previous versions [@fraillon_preparing_2020], and relevant studies has accepted the international validity of its proposal [@campos_digital_2024; @gebhardt_gender_2019; @karpinski_noncognitive_2023; @rohatgi_role_2016]. Since the tasks outlined in PISA battery are quite similar, it is likely that a two-dimensional approach would also be appropriate in its study. 

The dimensions of the DSE are not only relevant to contrast for theoretical reasons, but also because consideration of this approach has an impact on the distribution among groups. A series of studies using the two-dimensional ICILS model has shown that girls outperform boys in general DSE, but present lower scores on specialized DSE [@campos_digital_2024; @kaarakainen_differences_2017; @cusso-calabuig_effects_2018; @cai_gender_2017]. In turn, the literature consistently reports that students with low expectations of specialized self-efficacy sometimes score higher on standardized tests of digital skills [@aesaert_accuracy_2017; @weigold_measuring_2021]. 

In this study we have two main objectives. First, test the two-dimensional approach used by ICILS in the PISA battery in order to demonstrate that unidimensional digital self-efficacy can be consistently understood in a bidimensional frame. Second, evaluate the reliability and stability of constructs across genders and countries by analyzing invariance between groups, aiming to verify the external validation of the proposed digital self-efficacy batteries. Considering the previous statements, the hypotheses are the following: 

$H_{1}$: It is possible to identify two latent dimensions of digital self-efficacy (general and specialized) on PISA and ICILS.

$H_{2}$: The bi-dimensional measurement model of digital self-efficacy is equivalent across countries in ICILS and PISA.

$H_{3}$: The bi-dimensional measurement model of digital self-efficacy is equivalent between girls and boys.

$H_{4}$: General and Specialized DSE exhibit distinct patterns of association with gender and national context.
